meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Mixes conceptual understanding, code reading, debugging, and output prediction to build software engineering skills

front.content:
What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
Which one do you install to: (a) develop Java, (b) only run Java programs?

back.content:
JVM = Java Virtual Machine — executes bytecode (.class files). Platform-specific.
JRE = JVM + standard libraries (java.lang, java.util...) — needed to RUN programs.
JDK = JRE + dev tools (javac, javadoc, jar, jdb) — needed to DEVELOP.

(a) Install JDK to develop
(b) Install JRE (or JDK) to only run

Memory trick: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM

💡 In an interview: 'javac compiles .java → .class; java (JVM) executes .class'

Output:
2
1
2.5

Explanation:
• x / y = 5 / 2 → INTEGER division truncates decimal → 2 (not 2.5!)
• x % y = 5 % 2 → remainder after dividing → 1
• (double) x / y → cast x to 2.5 first, THEN divide → 2.5

🐛 Common Bug: Expecting 5/2 = 2.5 but getting 2. Fix: cast to double first.
💡 Modulo (%) is useful: check even/odd (n%2==0), check divisibility (n%10==0 means ends in 0)

front.content:
What are the 8 primitive data types in Java?
Name each with its size and use case.

back.content:
byte    → 1 byte  → status codes, KYC level (0-127)
short   → 2 bytes → branch codes, small counters
int     → 4 bytes → transaction count, IDs under 2 billion
long    → 8 bytes → account numbers, phone numbers, timestamps (needs 'L' suffix: 9876L)
float   → 4 bytes → interest rate display (needs 'f' suffix: 8.5f)
double  → 8 bytes → balance display, calculations (default decimal)
char    → 2 bytes → single character: 'D'=Debit, 'C'=Credit, 'S'=Savings
boolean → 1 bit   → flags: isActive, isFrozen, hasOverdraft

⚠️ NEVER use double for actual money math — use BigDecimal instead!

Output:
2147483647
-2147483648

😱 This is INTEGER OVERFLOW — Java wraps around silently, NO exception!

The bit pattern for 2,147,483,647 + 1 wraps to -2,147,483,648 (Integer.MIN_VALUE)

🐛 Bug scenario: Using 'int' for a bank account number that exceeds 2.1 billion — it wraps to negative!
Fix: Use 'long' (max: 9,223,372,036,854,775,807)

💡 Debugging tip: Always check data types when you see unexpected negative numbers in calculations.

front.content:
🔍 PREDICT THE OUTPUT — Pre vs Post Increment:

int i = 5;
System.out.println(i++);  // Line A
System.out.println(++i);  // Line B
System.out.println(i);    // Line C

back.content:
Output:
5   ← Line A: i++ is POST-increment. Returns 5, THEN i becomes 6.
7   ← Line B: ++i is PRE-increment. i becomes 7, THEN returns 7.
7   ← Line C: i is still 7.

Rule:
• i++ → use current value, THEN increment (Post: print first, add later)
• ++i → increment FIRST, THEN use new value (Pre: add first, print later)

🐛 Common Bug: Using i++ instead of ++i inside expressions leads to logic errors.
💡 Best practice: Keep increment statements on their own line to avoid confusion.

&& (AND): If LEFT side is FALSE → skip right side entirely
|| (OR):  If LEFT side is TRUE  → skip right side entirely

In the example:
• If user == null: short-circuits → user.isActive() is NEVER called
• Without null check: NullPointerException! Most common Java runtime error.

Why it matters:
1. Safety: prevents NullPointerException
2. Performance: skips expensive operations (DB query, API call) when not needed

💡 Rule: Always put the cheaper/safer check on the LEFT side of &&

Banking example:
if (account != null && account.getBalance() >= withdrawAmount && !account.isFrozen()) {
    processWithdrawal();
}

front.content:
What is the difference between break and continue in a loop?
Show with a code example.

back.content:
break   → EXITS the loop entirely (stops all iterations)
continue → SKIPS current iteration, moves to NEXT

Example — Processing transactions, skip negatives, stop on 0:
for (double txn : transactions) {
    if (txn == 0) break;      // end-of-data sentinel
    if (txn < 0) continue;    // skip invalid negative amounts
    totalDeposit += txn;
}

Output trace with [5000, -100, 3000, 0, 2000]:
• 5000 → added
• -100 → continue (skipped)
• 3000 → added
• 0   → break (exits, 2000 never processed)
Result: totalDeposit = 8000

💡 Think: break=STOP, continue=SKIP

front.content:
What is the difference between while and do-while?
When would you choose do-while?

back.content:
Bug: Loop condition uses <= instead of < → causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException!

For array of length 5, valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
With i <= 5, it tries scores[5] → doesn't exist → EXCEPTION!

Exception thrown:
java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5

✅ Fix: Change <= to <
for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(scores[i]);
}

💡 Debugging technique:
1. Read the exception message: 'Index 5 out of bounds for length 5'
2. Find which loop/access caused it
3. Check: is condition i < or i <=?

💡 To avoid this entirely: use enhanced for-each when you don't need the index.

front.content:
What is implicit widening vs explicit narrowing type conversion?
Show what gets LOST in narrowing.

back.content:
Widening (implicit) — automatic, no data loss:
byte → short → int → long → float → double

int i = 100;
long l = i;   // automatic, safe
double d = l; // automatic, safe

Narrowing (explicit) — must cast manually, CAN lose data:
double balance = 9.99;
int rounded = (int) balance;  // rounded = 9 (decimal TRUNCATED, not rounded!)

long bigNum = 300L;
byte b = (byte) bigNum; // b = 44 (300 % 256 = 44, wrapped around!)

🐛 Common Bug: Thinking (int)3.9 rounds to 4 — it TRUNCATES to 3!

💡 If you need rounding: Math.round(3.9) = 4
💡 If you need ceiling: (int)Math.ceil(3.1) = 4

Output:
false  ← a == b: different objects in heap (new creates new object)
true   ← a.equals(b): same characters
true   ← c == d: SAME object (String Pool/Interning! literals share reference)
true   ← c.equals(d): same characters

Why c == d is true:
String literals go into the String Pool. "RoboBank" is created once; c and d point to the SAME pooled object.

🐛 Bug in 99% of beginner Java code:
if (userInput == "yes") { ... }  // WRONG! May be false even if content matches

✅ Fix:
if ("yes".equals(userInput)) { ... }  // Note: literal.equals(var) avoids NPE if var is null

front.content: What are varargs in Java? Write a method that accepts varargs and show 3 different ways to call it.
Name 5 key methods from java.util.Arrays and what each does.

back.content:
import java.util.Arrays;

int[] nums = {5, 2, 8, 1, 9};

1. Arrays.sort(nums)
   → Sorts in ascending order: [1, 2, 5, 8, 9] (modifies ORIGINAL!)

2. Arrays.toString(nums)
   → Returns printable String: "[1, 2, 5, 8, 9]"
   (System.out.println(nums) just prints something like [I@6d06d69c)

3. Arrays.binarySearch(nums, 8)
   → Returns index of 8 in SORTED array: 3
   (MUST sort first! Undefined behavior on unsorted array)

4. Arrays.copyOf(nums, 3)
   → Returns new array: [1, 2, 5] (first 3 elements)

5. Arrays.fill(nums, 0)
   → Sets ALL elements to 0: [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]

💡 Arrays.equals(a, b) compares content — use instead of a==b for arrays.

Exception:
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.equals(Object)" because "pin" is null

Why: Calling a method (.equals()) on a null reference → NullPointerException

✅ Fix 1 — Null check first:
if (pin != null && pin.equals("1234")) { ... }

✅ Fix 2 — Literal on left (recommended!):
if ("1234".equals(pin)) { ... }
// If pin is null, "1234".equals(null) returns false — no exception!

💡 Debugging NullPointerException:
1. Read the stack trace — which line?
2. What variable on that line could be null?
3. Add null check or initialize properly

This is the most common Java runtime error. Always validate inputs!

Correct naming conventions:
Classes/Interfaces: PascalCase     → BankAccount, CustomerService
Methods:           camelCase       → calculateEMI(), isEligible()
Variables:         camelCase       → bankBalance, customerId
Constants:         UPPER_SNAKE     → MAX_ATTEMPTS, DEFAULT_RATE

What's WRONG:
a) int BankBalance      → BUG: starts with uppercase. Fix: int bankBalance
b) String customerID    → Acceptable, but prefer: customerId (ID → Id in camelCase)
c) final int maxattempts → BUG: constant should be UPPER_SNAKE. Fix: MAX_ATTEMPTS
d) void Withdraw()      → BUG: method starts with uppercase. Fix: void withdraw()

💡 Why it matters: Code reviews fail on naming. Inconsistent naming signals a junior mindset.
💡 Tools: Checkstyle, SonarQube enforce naming in real projects.

front.content:
What is platform independence in Java?
Trace the steps from .java file to execution on any OS.

back.content:
Platform independence = 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA)

Step-by-step:
1. You write: BankApp.java (human-readable source code)
2. javac compiles it: BankApp.class (bytecode — JVM instructions, NOT machine code)
3. JVM on any OS reads BankApp.class and JIT-compiles to native machine code
4. The SAME .class file runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android...

Why it matters in enterprise:
• Banking core systems built in Java run on Linux servers in data centers
• The same JAR file runs on developer Windows laptops, Linux QA servers, cloud containers
• No 'it works on my machine' problem for compiled code

Contrast with C/C++:
• C compiles directly to machine code (EXE on Windows)
• Must recompile separately for each OS/architecture

💡 Interview Q: 'Is Java compiled or interpreted?' Answer: BOTH — compiled to bytecode, then JIT-interpreted.

Output:
15000.0

😮 The array is UNCHANGED! Why?

In a for-each loop, 'e' is a COPY of the array element, not a reference to it.
Modifying 'e' does NOT modify the original array.

✅ Fix — Use index-based loop to modify array:
for (int i = 0; i < emi.length; i++) {
    emi[i] = emi[i] * 1.1;  // modifies original array
}
System.out.println(emi[0]);  // → 16500.0

💡 Rule:
• Use for-each to READ values from an array
• Use index-based for to MODIFY values in an array

This is a subtle but common bug — especially with primitive arrays.
